title: Starting with yourself
hook: the old manuals begin metta with oneself, the easiest proof that everyone wants to be happy

segments.voice: Yesterday, the four phrases: safe, happy, healthy, at ease. Your line was may you be at ease. Did someone get it silently as you passed? Day ninety-eight.
screen: `THE FOUR PHRASES — MAY YOU BE AT EASE.`

segments.voice: The week closes here: it began with the last long Jatakas and the end of the story camp, and it ends with metta, step by step. Quick test. Say to a friend: I hope you have a good day. Easy. Now say it to yourself, out loud: I hope I have a good day. For a lot of people, that second one feels strange. Embarrassing, even. Selfish. As if kindness is something you only hand outward. So here's a surprise from the old Buddhist manuals. When they teach metta step by step, the very first person they tell you to wish well is not your mother, not a teacher, not the world. It's you.
screen: `I HOPE YOU HAVE A GOOD DAY.` → `I HOPE I HAVE A GOOD DAY.` → `THE FIRST PERSON IS YOU.`

segments.voice: The manual is the Visuddhimagga, the Path of Purification, written by the monk Buddhaghosa in Sri Lanka around the fifth century. In its ninth chapter, on loving-kindness, it says to begin by wishing yourself well: may I be happy, may I be free from suffering. Why start there? Not because you're the most important person in the room. The reason is almost the opposite. When you wish yourself well, you notice something plain: I want to be happy. I don't want to suffer. And the manual says, use that as your example. Everyone else wants exactly the same thing, just as much. Your own wish is the easiest proof. The manual backs this up with a teaching found in the Pali texts. King Pasenadi and Queen Mallika, the story goes, admit to each other that nobody is dearer to them than themselves. The Buddha doesn't scold them. He answers with a verse, in substance: search every direction, and you won't find anyone dearer to a person than their own self; since each one holds themselves that dear, whoever loves themselves should harm no one. So starting with yourself isn't the selfish shortcut. It's the doorway. The manual even says that metta for yourself alone isn't the goal. It's where you learn what the wish feels like, so you can hand it on. That's why this practice matters on a hard day. The voice in your head that says you don't deserve kindness is exactly the voice this practice answers. You count too.
screen: `THE PATH OF PURIFICATION, CHAPTER NINE.` · `MAY I BE HAPPY.` · `YOUR WISH IS THE PROOF.` · `NOBODY DEARER THAN ONESELF.` · then, large: `YOU COUNT TOO.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your hands rest somewhere comfortable, maybe one over your heart. Breathe a few times. Now offer the phrases to yourself, slowly. May I be safe. May I be happy. May I be healthy. May I live with ease. If it feels awkward, that's normal; let the awkwardness be there too. If it helps, picture yourself as a small child and say the words to them. Keep repeating, gently, with space between. The bell holds the time.
Starting with yourself. The old manuals begin metta with you: your own wish to be happy shows you what everyone wants.
Your line: you count too. Today, when you catch yourself being harsh with yourself, answer with one phrase: may I be at ease. Day ninety-eight.

howItsDone: In many Buddhist metta practices, especially those following the Visuddhimagga, practitioners begin by wishing themselves well before extending the wish to others.

tell them to love themselves less.

original.note: Pali: oneself; in the verse to Pasenadi, no one is dearer to a person than attā, one's own self.

trapdoor: what you thought: self-love as a wellness trend.
what it means: starting with yourself to learn the wish, then handing it on to everyone.
what a scholar hears: Visuddhimagga IX cites the verse from Udana 5.1 (also SN 3.8), spoken after Pasenadi and Mallika's conversation, to explain why metta begins with oneself.
